question.text: Will Judge McFadden have granted Comey's motion to dismiss the D.C. criminal information by November 13, 2026?
question.resolution_criteria: This question resolves Yes if, on or before November 13, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia issues an order in United States v. Comey, No. 1:26-cr-00229-TNM, granting James Comey's motion to dismiss the criminal information (ECF No. 11, including any amended or refiled version of that motion) and dismissing the criminal information in its entirety, with or without prejudice; an order granting the motion only in part, so that any count of the information survives, resolves No. It resolves No if the Court denies that motion or has issued no order granting it by that date. Resolution is based on the case docket in 1:26-cr-00229-TNM (case filings are compiled at https://www.nacdl.org/brief/United-States-v-Comey-(2)) or, if the docket is unavailable, on reporting by [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions).
question.fine_print: Dismissal of the criminal information on any other basis — for example, a motion by the government to dismiss, or the return of a grand jury indictment that supersedes the information — does not count as granting ECF No. 11, including where the Court denies that motion as moot. If the Court issues an order granting ECF No. 11 on or before November 13, 2026, but the order becomes public only after that date, the question still resolves Yes.

research:
I found no order on Comey's motion to dismiss (ECF No. 11) as of November 2. The October 30 hearing ended with the motion taken under advisement. McFadden openly questioned whether it was premature to rule while the government is still seeking a grand jury indictment, and an indictment would likely make the motion moot. Under the fine print, a denial as moot resolves No.

## 1. Resolution source
- 2026-11-02 (fetched): The NACDL tracker lists only four filings: ECF 1, the information (10/05/26); ECF 6, the first motion to dismiss plus a request for an emergency hearing (10/09/26); ECF 11, the motion to dismiss (10/16/26); and ECF 12, the government's response (10/23/26). It shows no order on ECF 11 and doesn't yet list ECF 14, the unsealing order. [NACDL](https://www.nacdl.org/brief/United-States-v-Comey-(2))
- The CourtListener docket API needs a login, so I couldn't read the live docket directly.

## 2. Current status
- 2026-10-30: McFadden heard argument and did not rule. He said the case turns on "very novel issues" and asked, "Aren't we getting a little ahead of ourselves?" He questioned both sides on whether an indictment would make the issue moot. [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doj-james-comey-information-espionage-act-hearing/), [Spokesman/Bloomberg](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/oct/30/doj-seeks-grand-jury-indictment-of-comey-on-defens/)
- 2026-10-30: He did not bar the government from going to a grand jury, calling it the government's choice. He also said that if a grand jury refused to indict, the proceedings would have been futile, and joked that "ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days." [NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/james-comey-team-court-seeking-toss-third-doj-case-longtime-trump-foe-rcna606394)
- One summary said McFadden "seemed inclined to rule for the defense" on whether an indictment was required, but noted that Comey could renew his limitations argument after any indictment. [search summary; WaPo](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/30/judge-weighs-whether-justice-dept-violated-statute-charging-james-comey/)
- So far nothing settles the question.

## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- 2026-11-02: In a separate D.D.C. case, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui dismissed a criminal complaint against former FBI officials Floris and Benavides, citing "weaponization." It shows how that courthouse is treating similar prosecutions but is not this case. [NY Post](https://nypost.com/2026/11/02/us-news/dc-federal-judge-tosses-case-against-fbi-officials-accused-of-lying-about-hunter-biden-laptop/)
- 2026-10-31: Commentary argued the information "might get tossed." [Townhall](https://townhall.com/news/mattvespa/2026/10/31/the-james-comey-national-security-leak-indictment-might-get-tossed-n2685635)
- 2026-10-30: The prosecutor told the court, "We are still going to the grand jury very diligently." DOJ said it is considering charges for conduct through April 2017, which would fall inside the limitations period and so would not depend on the information question. [Spokesman](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/oct/30/doj-seeks-grand-jury-indictment-of-comey-on-defens/), [NBC](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/james-comey-team-court-seeking-toss-third-doj-case-longtime-trump-foe-rcna606394)
- 2026-10-30: McFadden warned he would be "extremely frustrated" by a "dawn raid" to arrest Comey. [ABC7](https://abc7news.com/story/attorneys-james-comey-return-court-fight-dojs-efforts-charge-3rd-time/20000350/)
- 2026-10-16: According to Comey's filing, DOJ had planned to seek an indictment on October 9 but agreed to wait 30 days. That pause ends in early November: ABC says November 5, and 30 days from October 9 would be November 8. [Spokesman](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/oct/30/doj-seeks-grand-jury-indictment-of-comey-on-defens/)
- I found no reporting from October 31 to November 2 of an indictment, a ruling, or any new filing in 1:26-cr-00229.

## 4. Base rates
- I found no data on how often a judge grants a statute-of-limitations dismissal of a waiverless information within two weeks of argument. NACDL calls the issue novel.
- Federal judges often deny pretrial motions as moot once a superseding indictment arrives. McFadden's mootness questions point toward waiting rather than ruling.
- Earlier Comey prosecutions: the Eastern District of Virginia case was dismissed about two months after indictment (November 24, 2025). As of late October, the North Carolina judge had not ruled on Comey's motions.

## 5. Other forecasts
Prices as of 2026-11-02 18:09 UTC:
- Kalshi, "Will James Comey's national defense information case be dismissed?" for 1:26-cr-00229 (D.D.C.): 22% before January 1, 2027, 90% before July 1, 2027. This is the closest market, but it is broader than this question. It likely counts any dismissal, including on the government's own motion, and covers a longer window.
- Kalshi, the general "Comey case dismissed" market (case not specified): 27% before January 1, 2027.
- Polymarket, "Comey charges dropped by December 31?": 39%. It doesn't specify which case.
- No market covers the November 13 deadline or a dismissal specifically by grant of ECF 11.

## 6. Upcoming events before November 13
- About November 5 to 8: the agreed 30-day pause on seeking an indictment ends, and DOJ is expected to go to a grand jury.
- If an indictment comes back, ECF 11 would likely be denied as moot or overtaken by a new motion, which resolves No.
- If the grand jury declines to indict, or DOJ doesn't seek one, McFadden could rule on the merits. Reporting suggests he is skeptical of the government's position.
- Possible new filings: DOJ notices about grand jury status or additional charges, or supplemental briefing. None found so far.
- The November 3 midterms make the political backdrop noisier, but nothing is scheduled in court.

## Comey D.C. case: research notes as of 2026-11-02

**Bottom line:** I found no order on ECF No. 11 as of November 2. At the October 30 argument, McFadden chose to wait rather than rule, and let prosecutors keep seeking an indictment. If the case ends because the government moves to dismiss, because an indictment replaces the information, or because ECF 11 is denied as moot, the question resolves No.

### 1. Resolution source

### 4. Base rates
- I found no direct base rate. Federal judges rarely grant pretrial motions to dismiss within two weeks of argument, especially when they have said they would rather wait for prosecutors to act. Here the judge called the issues novel, and the government argued the motion was premature.

- I found no market specifically on McFadden granting ECF 11 by November 13.

### 6. Upcoming events before November 13
- 2026-11-05 (Thursday): The reported last day for an indictment under the Speedy Trial timeline. Three outcomes are possible:
  - An indictment would probably make ECF 11 moot (No).
  - No indictment could lead the government to dismiss, or to a Speedy Trial dismissal (No).
  - McFadden could rule on the merits (the only path to Yes).
- Any grand jury no-bill: D.C. grand juries have repeatedly refused politically sensitive indictments.
- The pending E.D.N.C. case and the Fourth Circuit appeal of the E.D. Va. dismissal are not directly relevant.

forecasts.reasoning:
**(a) Time left and what Yes requires.** About 11 days remain, to November 13, 2026. For Yes, Judge McFadden must issue an order granting ECF No. 11 and dismissing both counts of the information. Partial grants, mootness denials, government dismissals and supersession by indictment all resolve No.

**(b) Status quo.** The motion has been under advisement since October 30, with no order. If nothing changes, the answer is No.

**(c) Base rate.** I found no data on fast merits grants of pretrial limitations dismissals, especially while the government says it is actively seeking an indictment. Within two weeks of argument, such grants are rare, around 5-10%. The closest market is Kalshi's 22% for any dismissal of this case before January 1. That covers a broader set of outcomes (including a voluntary government dismissal) over a window roughly five times longer.

**(d) Evidence.**
- For Yes:
  - At the October 30 hearing, McFadden was skeptical of the government's "waiverless information" maneuver.
  - The Washington Post summary said he "seemed inclined to rule for the defense" on whether an indictment was required.
  - D.D.C. grand juries and judges have been hostile to similar cases. On November 2, Magistrate Judge Faruqui dismissed the Floris and Benavides complaint.
  - McFadden himself noted that an indictment was no sure thing.
- For No:
  - On October 30 he asked, "Aren't we getting a little ahead of ourselves?" and raised mootness with both sides.
  - He explicitly left the grand jury route open to the government.
  - DOJ says it is "still going to the grand jury very diligently," with the pause ending around November 5-8.
  - An indictment would most likely lead to a mootness denial or a renewed motion, which resolves No.
  - DOJ may also add charges based on later conduct that fall inside the limitations period.

**(e) Scenarios.**
- No: A grand jury returns an indictment around November 5-10. McFadden denies ECF 11 as moot or simply leaves it pending. Alternatively, there is no news by November 13 and the motion is still pending.
- Yes: The grand jury declines to indict, or DOJ stalls past its own deadline. McFadden then promptly issues an opinion granting the motion before DOJ can voluntarily dismiss, around November 10-13.

**(f) Moving from base rate to forecast.** I put the chance of no indictment by about November 8 at around 35%. Given no indictment, the chance McFadden grants by November 13 is around 25%, since he might wait, or DOJ might dismiss first. That gives about 9%. A small chance of an early merits ruling adds a little, while the overall preference for the status quo trims it. I land at about 7%.

Probability: 7%

(a) About 11 days remain, until November 13, 2026. For Yes, Judge McFadden must issue an order granting ECF No. 11 and dismissing the whole information. A denial as moot after an indictment, a dismissal on the government's own motion, or a partial grant all resolve No.

(b) Status quo: the motion is under advisement. McFadden signaled he would rather wait to see what the grand jury does. If nothing changes, the result is No.

(c) Base rate: judges who take a novel pretrial dismissal motion under advisement while the government says it is actively seeking a superseding indictment rarely grant it within two weeks. They usually wait and then deny as moot. I put the reference-class rate around 5-10%.

(d) Evidence:
- **For Yes:** On October 30, McFadden was described as skeptical of the government's maneuver. The Washington Post summary said he "seemed inclined to rule for the defense" on whether an indictment is required. His "ham sandwiches are harder to indict" remark signals that a grand jury no-bill is plausible. DC grand juries have recently refused politically charged indictments. On November 2, a D.D.C. magistrate dismissed a similar complaint against former FBI officials. The government's window to indict (about November 5-8) closes before the deadline. If no indictment arrives, McFadden could rule quickly.

An indictment leads to denial as moot, which resolves No. Even if the grand jury balks, DOJ might dismiss the information itself, or McFadden might take longer than a few days to write an opinion on "very novel issues." Kalshi puts any dismissal of this case before January 1, 2027 at only 22%, and that market is broader than this question.

(e) Scenarios:
- **No:** DOJ obtains an indictment around November 5. McFadden denies ECF 11 as moot, and Comey files a new motion against the indictment.
- **Yes:** The grand jury declines to indict, or DOJ misses its window. McFadden promptly issues an opinion holding that a waiverless information does not satisfy the limitations period, and dismisses both counts before November 13.

(f) My estimate breaks down as follows:
- The chance there is no indictment by about November 8 is roughly 35%.
- Given that, the chance McFadden fully grants the motion by November 13, rather than seeing DOJ dismiss or waiting longer, is about 30-35%.
- There is a small added chance he rules on the merits before any indictment.

That gives roughly 11-13%. I shade down slightly toward the Kalshi anchor, since that market covers a longer window and any form of dismissal and still sits at only 22%. I end at about 10%, slightly above the base rate because of the judge's apparent skepticism and the real chance of a no-bill.
